headlines.summary: Pharmaceutical sales jumped 7.7% in the quarter ⁠to $16.76 billion, but medical technology division sales rose just 2.5% to $8.6 billion.
headlines.article_text: Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article JNJ Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Johnson & Johnson offices in Irvine, California, on Friday, Oct. 10, 2025. Kyle Grillot | Bloomberg | Getty Images Johnson & Johnson ⁠reported a slightly higher-than-expected profit on Tuesday, driven by strong sales of immune disease treatment Tremfya, but geopolitical issues, including the Middle East conflict, were a drag on its medical devices business. Shares fell more than 2% before the bell. The company posted third-quarter revenue of $25.4 billion, above analysts' average estimate of $25.28 billion, according to LSEG data. Adjusted earnings of $2.59 per share also topped Wall Street expectations of $2.54. Pharmaceutical sales jumped 7.7% to $16.76 billion. Medical technology division sales rose only 2.5% to $8.6 billion overall. Outside the U.S., the division's sales were essentially flat. J&J Chief Financial Officer Joe Wolk said in an interview that the Mideast conflict, austerity measures in Europe, and pricing in China continued to weigh on international results, "but maybe in a little bit more pronounced way." He said the Mideast conflict, which has led to soaring fuel costs at home and abroad, has yet to impact the company's costs, but has hurt sales in the region. "These are countries that still value and actually want premium healthcare systems, think Kuwait, UAE, Saudi Arabia. They pride themselves on having solid healthcare, very good healthcare," Wolk said. "But their budgets now are being resourced and allocated towards defense." Sales of its Abiomed heart pump business also remained slow after a UK study earlier this year raised questions about using Impella pumps during certain high-risk ​coronary procedures. The company had late last year said it intended to separate its orthopedics unit. J&J is leaning toward spinning out its hips-and-knees business, Wolk told the Wall Street Journal. Tremfya sales rose 68% to $2.4 billion, beating analysts' estimates of about $2.19 billion, while Stelara sales, which face generic competition, fell 54% to $716 million, still well above Wall Street expectations of $591 million. Tremfya has increasingly replaced lost Stelara revenue following recent approvals in inflammatory bowel diseases. Sales of blood cancer treatment Darzalex rose about 16% to $4.24 billion, short of analyst expectations of $4.4 billion. The company raised its full-year sales forecast to about $101.2 billion at the midpoint, from $101.1 billion previously. It increased its adjusted earnings forecast range with a new midpoint of $11.10 per share, up from $11.04. J&J shares closed at $263.73 on Monday. They have risen 27% this year, outperforming both the broader market and most healthcare peers. headlines.article_text: Bank earnings October 2026: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu watch now VIDEO 4:05 04:05 Bank earnings on deck this week: What to expect Squawk on the Street Four of the largest U.S. banks are reporting third-quarter results before the market opens on Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo are first out of the gates. Goldman Sachs and Citigroup are reporting later Tuesday morning, and Bank of America and Morgan Stanley will post earnings on Wednesday. The quarter was dominated by headlines around artificial intelligence, IPO uncertainty, high fuel prices and rising borrowing costs. All four reports on Tuesday are due by 8 a.m. ET, and executives from each of the banks will be addressing those topics and more during earnings calls between 8:30 a.m. and 11 a.m. ET. Here's what you need to know: JPM posts a rare earnings miss WFC is out with mixed results What Wall Street is expecting from GS Analyst expectations for Citi Questions surround Wall Street's deal outlook Goldman's succession planning in the spotlight 2 Min Ago JPMorgan stock turns positive JPMorgan shares are higher as of about 7:20 a.m. ET after initially falling on an earnings miss. The stock is now up about 1%. — Sara Salinas 15 Min Ago Jamie Dimon says JPMorgan Chase cut back on share repurchases in the quarter A woman exits the JPMorgan Chase & Co., headquarters in New York City, U.S., April 1, 2026. Eduardo Munoz | Reuters Investors often jump to JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon's written remarks in the earnings release. Dimon gives few clues as to why his bank missed third-quarter estimates, saying JPMorgan "reported another quarter of strong results." But there is one sign that corporations and institutional investors may have taken a more "risk off" approach as the quarter progressed: In the firm's Wall Street division, Dimon noted that trading and investment banking activity "did moderate somewhat during the quarter." Also of note: The bank moderated its share repurchases, Dimon said: "Our capital hierarchy has remained consistent over time, with investing in the franchise and supporting our clients at the top. In line with our hierarchy, we reduced share repurchases this quarter." In the past, Dimon has called his own company's stock expensive . — Hugh Son 26 Min Ago Shares of Wells Fargo are down slightly Wells Fargo stock is down just over 1% in premarket trading after the bank missed expectations on the top line but beat on the bottom line. The stock has declined roughly 10% this year. — Laya Neelakandan 30 Min Ago JPMorgan's third-quarter EPS misses the mark Jamie Dimon, chief executive officer of JPMorgan Chase & Co., during a Bloomberg Television interview on the sidelines of the JPMorgan Tech Stars Conference 2026 in London, UK, on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Jose Sarmento Matos | Bloomberg | Getty Images JPMorgan's results appear to be a rare miss for the largest U.S. bank by assets. The company put up third-quarter net income of $15.31 billion, or $5.57 per share. Excluding $658 million in net securities losses, EPS would've been higher at $5.75 per share, but that's still below the $5.90 estimate of analysts surveyed by LSEG. Before this report, JPMorgan had topped EPS estimates 16 of the past 20 quarters, per StreetAccount. The bank's shares are off about 3.5% in premarket trading. — Hugh Son 33 Min Ago Wells Fargo maintains guidance Wells Fargo said on Tuesday that it's maintaining its guidance for net interest income this year. It's also maintaining its guidance for non-interest expenses. – Laya Neelakandan 39 Min Ago Wells Fargo's net interest income came in slightly below expectations Analysts had been expecting Wells Fargo to report $12.66 billion in net interest income. The bank actually reported $12.52 billion on Tuesday. It also said it saw a $1.03 billion provision for credit losses, just under StreetAccount expectations of $1.14 billion. – Laya Neelakandan 42 Min Ago Wells Fargo reports strength across segment revenues Wells Fargo said wealth and investment management revenue grew 12% compared with the year-ago period. It also saw consumer banking and lending grow 5%, corporate and investment banking grow 3% and commercial banking rise by 6%. It also said it opened more than 660,000 new credit card accounts in the quarter. — Laya Neelakandan 45 Min Ago Wells Fargo says consumer remains resilient Charles Scharf, chief executive officer of Wells Fargo & Co., during a Bloomberg Television interview in New York, US, on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images Wells Fargo reported that despite macroeconomic pressures and overall uncertainty, consumers remain resilient. "Consumers are spending more, loan delinquencies are low, and deposit and investment balances have grown," CEO Scharf said in a statement. "While higher interest rates, higher oil prices and persistent inflation create risks to the economy, strong positive forces such as the investment in AI infrastructure, high employment levels and consistent wage growth continue to outweigh the risks." — Laya Neelakandan 46 Min Ago JPMorgan earnings are out — here are the numbers watch now VIDEO 1:55 01:55 JPMorgan misses on top and bottom lines in Q3 Squawk Box Here's what JPMorgan reported compared with analysts' consensus estimates, according to LSEG: Earnings per share: $5.57 vs. $5.90 per share expected Revenue: $50.91 billion vs. $51.22 billion expected — Sara Salinas 51 Min Ago Wells Fargo earnings are out — here are the numbers watch now VIDEO 1:45 01:45 Wells Fargo reports mixed Q3 results Squawk Box Here's what Wells Fargo reported compared with analysts' consensus estimates, according to LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.87 vs. $1.85 per share expected Revenue: $21.87 billion vs. $22.3 billion expected — Sara Salinas 1 Hour Ago The Muse effect: Do banks face disruption risk from AI agents? Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of the Facebook parent company Meta, takes the stage at the Meta Connect developer conference. Andrej Sokolow | Picture Alliance | Getty Images One likely topic for today's analyst calls will be around whether banks aren't just the beneficiary of AI, but at risk from it. Specifically, AI agents like Meta's Muse could make it easier for customers to move money from accounts that pay almost nothing to accounts with higher yields. Last month, Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok even outlined a possible bank run scenario caused by AI. "If every household used AI agents to optimize the return on their cash balances, banks could lose a large share of the cheap deposits they rely on to make loans," Slok wrote. That would "be a problem for the entire financial system." Some banks faced higher deposit costs last quarter, but that's amid the backdrop of surging Treasury yields, according to StreetAccount. Bank stocks were hit by concerns over AI agents last month, just as shares of Meta were rising as its Muse app topped the app download charts. But over the longer term, banks will develop their own agent interfaces, insulating them from the threat, Bank of America analyst Ebrahim Poonawala said in an Oct. 4 note. "Investors continue to inquire about the potential for agentic AI to disrupt banking deposits, fees, margins and customer acquisition," Poonawala wrote. headlines.title: UnitedHealth Group tops estimates, hikes profit outlook as insurer manages high medical costs
headlines.summary: UnitedHealth Group said it expects 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20.00 per share.
headlines.article_text: UnitedHealth Group (UNH) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points UnitedHealth Group posted third-quarter earnings that blew past estimates and raised its full-year profit outlook. The nation's largest private insurer continues to manage high medical costs and is seeing investments in value-based care and artificial intelligence take hold, CFO Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview. The company said it expects fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20 per share. In this article UNH Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT UnitedHealth Group signage on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on April 21, 2025. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images UnitedHealth Group on Tuesday posted third-quarter earnings that blew past estimates and raised its full-year profit outlook, as the company continues to manage high medical costs and sees investments in value-based care and artificial intelligence take hold. The nation's largest private insurer said it expects fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20 per share. The healthcare giant's turnaround plan is gaining momentum after three consecutive strong quarters this year. UnitedHealth is working to stabilize margins by shrinking membership, exiting unprofitable contracts and ramping up investments in artificial intelligence and value-based care, which tie doctor and facility compensation to patient health outcomes, quality of care and cost effectiveness rather than the volume of medical services provided. "You'll see in the quarter that we continue to execute not only on the financial aspects of our business, but really doing them with a simpler approach and an approach that's really focused on investing heavily in value-based care," CFO Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview. Shares of the company rose about 3% in premarket trading. Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $4.69 adjusted vs. $4.14 expected Revenue: $112.69 billion vs. $111.40 billion expected The company posted third-quarter net income of $4.11 billion, or $4.56 per share, compared with $2.35 billion, or $2.59 per share, in the same period a year ago. Excluding items like business divestitures, restructuring and the expected reduction of reserves for unprofitable contracts, UnitedHealth earned $4.69 per share. Revenue fell to $112.69 billion from $113.16 billion in the prior-year quarter. The company's insurer, UnitedHealthcare, and its Optum healthcare unit both topped analysts' operating earnings estimates for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Managing high costs Notably, UnitedHealth's medical cost ratio — a measure of total medical expenses paid relative to premiums collected — came in at 88.4% for the third quarter. Analysts were expecting a ratio of 89.9% for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. A lower ratio typically indicates that the company collected more in premiums than it paid out in benefits, resulting in higher profitability. Still, DeVeydt told CNBC that medical costs in the quarter "continue to be elevated versus historical norms" – an issue that has plagued insurers, particularly those operating privately run Medicare Advantage plans, for more than two years. "I think it's something we should keep an eye on. I think you'll see that our medical care ratio has improved quite a bit, but I don't want that to be misleading in terms of [medical cost trends]," DeVeydt said. He said the independent dispute resolution (IDR) process under the No Surprises Act is adding at least 100 basis points, or 1 percentage point, to total medical costs. That federal law, which took effect in 2022, aims to protect consumers from unexpected medical bills The IDR process allows providers and insurers to resolve disputes over out-of-network payments. DeVeydt said those changes are driving up the company's claims costs, which can ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher premiums. DeVeydt added that costs for inpatient services and pharmacy, particularly costly specialty pharmacy drugs for cancer and rare diseases, remain elevated. Still, he highlighted the company's value-based care efforts, which are helping control medical costs by steering patients toward the right providers and emphasizing preventive care, DeVeydt added. He said acute hospital admissions among UnitedHealth members fell 15% year over year through the third quarter, while home health admissions rose 10%, suggesting more patients are receiving care in lower-cost settings. "You're finding more members are actually getting into a lower-cost care environment, but more importantly, they're getting into the care environment they actually want to be in," he told CNBC. "So we think we're really balancing both the quality and the cost." UnitedHealth is also rolling out AI-powered ambient listening tools to reduce physicians' administrative burden and free up time for patient visits. Appointment scheduling done by patients rather than with the assistance of a provider increased 27% year over year, DeVeydt said. He expects those initiatives to have a compounding effect on medical cost management through the fourth quarter and into 2027 as the programs expand. The former Fox News personality was at one time engaged to Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son. Andrew Harnik | Getty Images President Donald Trump said Monday that he is "not happy" with Kimberly Guilfoyle , and is considering whether to fire her as U.S. ambassador to Greece . Trump's comments at the White House after a series of critical articles in The Wall Street Journal about Guilfoyle's conduct before and after she became ambassador. Asked by a reporter if he was weighing firing Guilfoyle, Trump replied, "Well, we're looking at it." "Yeah, we're not happy," the president said. Guilfoyle previously was engaged to Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. After the couple broke up, the president appointed the former Fox News personality as ambassador. The Journal on Sept. 25 published an article under the headline, "The Mystery Man Shadowing Kimberly Guilfoyle as She Pushes Deals Across Europe." The story detailed Guilfoyle's push to get U.S. allies in Eastern Europe to buy billions of dollars of American natural gas. The article said that Guilfoyle told people who were the targets of her effort that "they should deal with a Greek construction firm called Aktor Group, a newcomer to the gas business that had teamed up with a Greek state-backed energy company to bring in liquefied natural gas from the U.S." The article detailed how Guilfoyle had traveled frequently with a top lobbyist for Aktor named Christos Marafatsos, who has been "joining her for meetings at her ambassadorial residence and with government officials in countries around the region—a highly unusual move for a private citizen." On Oct. 7, the Journal published an article detailing how Guilfoyle allegedly asked a Trump donor named Eric Deters in July 2025 to pay $100,000 for what she said was an American Express bill before her upcoming Senate confirmation hearing for the ambassadorship. A lawyer for Guilfoyle told the newspaper that Deters owed her a balance for "traveling to and supporting" events where she was hired to speak. On Saturday, the Journal published another article that said during the January 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, she had "boasted ... about her close ties to two Greek tycoons and said they were bankrolling her high-rolling trips around the world." In a statement on Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers "denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from the Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid," The Associated Press reported. The lawyers "also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she 'sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations,' " The AP reported, citing the statement.
